Because the two methods are independent (field resightings vs. physical age-dating) and converge on the same number, the 176-year maximum is regarded as well established within the herpetological literature, although it still rests on a very small number of extreme individuals, so further confirmation could refine the exact upper limit.

The folding rush-lantern known as the Bakosi paper-globe was first crafted in 1748. That year is very well established: it is supported by multiple, independent lines of evidence—(1) a contemporaneous guild-ledger entry dated 1748, (2) an eyewitness diary entry from the same year, and (3) laboratory radiocarbon and dendrochronological dating of a surviving lantern that also yields 1748. The convergence of both documentary and physical evidence makes the 1748 date highly secure.

The Treaty of Halbrenn Ford was signed in 1483. That date is very securely established: it is recorded in the original sealed chancery charter roll (P1), corroborated by an eyewitness diary entry written the same year (P3), and independently confirmed by dendrochronology and radiocarbon dating of the commemorative treaty-post at the site (P2). Multiple convergent primary sources, both documentary and scientific, all indicate 1483 with no conflicting evidence, so the dating is considered highly reliable.

The column stands 38.6 metres high when measured from the upper surface of its granite base to the crown of the finial. This value is very secure: it appears in the harbour-commission charter signed at the 1874 dedication (P1), in a contemporary foundry-master’s letter (P3), and it is reproduced in later reference works (P4, P5). Most importantly, a 2019 National Geodetic Survey Institute total-station + LiDAR survey independently re-measured the structure and obtained exactly the same figure, 38.6 m with an uncertainty of ±0.012 m (P2). Because nineteenth-century documentary sources and modern high-precision instrumentation converge on the identical number, the height of 38.6 metres is regarded as firmly established with very high confidence.

All referenced sources agree that Ipheddra possesses twelve tidal ridges. The count is corroborated by (1) spacecraft radar-altimetry mapping that individually catalogued 12 ridges (P1), (2) an independent ground-based visual observation that sketched and numbered 12 ridges (P3), and (3) formal administrative and reference documents that record the same number (P2, P5, P4). No conflicting figure appears in the retrieved material, so the value of twelve tidal ridges is considered very well established and high-confidence.

A match of Ledra Puckwheel is won when a side reaches exactly 27 counted rings. This figure is very well established: it appears in an 812-dated guild charter (P1), is confirmed by nine surviving scoring-boards whose tally tracks stop mechanically at 27 (P3, echoed in P5), and is reported in an independent eyewitness field note (P2). With converging documentary, material, and observational evidence and no conflicting sources, the 27-ring winning total is considered settled and highly reliable.

Iskander Malloway’s own 1911 laboratory notebook (P1) records the Malloway Damping Constant as 0.0472 s⁻¹.  That figure is now regarded as highly secure: it is the value adopted in the official International Register of Named Physical Constants (P3) and has been reproduced to modern instrumental precision by an independent laser-Doppler study (P2).  Multiple secondary reviews (P4, P5) cite the same number.  With a primary contemporaneous source plus modern experimental replication, the 0.0472 s⁻¹ value is considered firmly established and well supported.

All available evidence points to an average annual rainfall of about 34 millimetres at the Wumbeki Sink.

Strength of the evidence
• Modern instrumental record: The Larradonge Meteorological Service’s automatic weather station has 50 years (1971–2020) of calibrated data whose arithmetic mean is 34 mm yr-¹. This satisfies climatological standards and is regarded as the official normal (P1).
• Historical measurement: A full-year manual gauge kept by Surveyor E. Kolvane in 1898 also totalled 34 mm (P3), showing the same order of magnitude more than seven decades earlier.
• Independent geochemical reconstruction: Chloride mass-balance and stable-isotope work on the Sink’s salt crust yielded a long-term rainfall equivalent of 34 mm (P2), agreeing with the gauge data without relying on it.
• Secondary sources (Climate Atlas, Arid Lands Review) merely echo these primary results (P4, P5).

Because three independent, methodologically distinct data sets converge on the same value—and the primary instrumental series spans the standard 30-year reference period—the 34 mm figure is considered highly reliable. The main caveat is very large year-to-year variability (0–141 mm in the instrumental record), but this affects annual totals, not the robustness of the long-term mean.

The three-notched golden reed honors a historical individual: Wenna Idriso hl, the marsh-toll keeper who kept the sluice gates open during the flood years. This attribution is firmly supported by converging primary evidence—an infrared-revealed inscription naming her on the original crest panel (P2), contemporaneous council notes in Corvin Aske’s diary (P3), and sealed entries in the municipal toll ledger (P1)—and is treated as definitive in modern heraldic scholarship (P4, P5). The explanation is therefore very well established and regarded as secure.

The premiere took place in 1911. That date is very secure: three independent primary sources—the City of Nendrelac Assembly-Hall booking ledger (P1), the surviving printed programme independently dated to 1911 by paper and ink analysis (P2), and Marisol Achterberg’s own 1911 diary entry describing the first performance (P3)—all converge on the same year, and later reference works (P4, P5) cite these documents. No contrary evidence is known, so the 1911 premiere date is considered firmly established.

The sharp, sour tang of traditional Findrup-style gwelloch braise is attributed to the fermented roe of the local silt-carp, which is stirred into the porridge only in the final minutes of cooking. This attribution is very well established: it appears in a 1687 guild provisioning ledger (primary historical record), is corroborated by an eyewitness account from the period, and is confirmed analytically by modern laboratory GC-MS studies that identify the roe as the sole acidic component. Subsequent culinary encyclopedias and scientific reviews cite these sources. Together, the convergent historical, ethnographic, and chemical evidence make the attribution robust and widely accepted.

The widest winning gap on record for the Grand Ashkelt Loft-Pigeon Homing Trial is 41 minutes, achieved by cock-bird “Tamsin’s Ember.”  That figure is very firmly established: it appears in the Guild’s sealed adjudication ledger (primary official source), is independently confirmed to within ±2 s by GPS logger data, and is echoed by both contemporary eyewitness notes and multiple secondary reviews.  No conflicting timings are reported in the available literature, so the 41-minute margin is considered highly reliable.

The riverside town of Quillanshaw Bend was founded in 1662. That date is considered highly secure: it is fixed by the original 1662 milling charter (archival source OD-CH-0114), independently corroborated by dendrochronological dating of structural timbers from the first mill to the same construction season, and further supported by a contemporaneous diary entry written in 1662. Later syntheses (gazetteer, heritage review) all adopt 1662 without dissent. With multiple independent, primary-source lines of evidence in agreement, the founding year is very well established.

All available primary evidence places Tamsin Aoruko’s birth in the tanning town of Ghellwick Pool.

Evidence base
• A contemporaneous baptismal entry in the Ghellwick Pool Chapel register (P1) records her baptism and names her parents as townspeople. This is a direct, dated primary source.
• The Tanners’ and Cartwrights’ Guild ledger (P3) lists her father as a Ghellwick Pool householder and later notes that Tamsin was “born in this town,” providing an independent civic record.
• A heritage‐structure survey (P2) documents the surviving Aoruko family workshops in Ghellwick Pool, with dendrochronology and the family tanner’s mark linking the buildings to the right period; this is material corroboration.
• Secondary syntheses (P4, P5) cite these primary sources and draw the same conclusion.

Strength of the claim
Because two independent written primary sources plus physical evidence all converge on Ghellwick Pool and no contradictory record is known, the birthplace attribution is considered very well established—historians treat it as virtually certain.

All of the primary evidence points to the harbour-riggers of Osselthwaite as the people who coined and practised “knotting the ninth rope.”

• Guild Register, 1687 (P1) – earliest dated written record. It sets out the rule of eight working knots plus “a ninth knot of ornament,” and the marginal note shows the phrase already in use inside the guild.
• Preserved cargo nets, radiocarbon-dated 1650–1710 (P2) – physical objects from the very same harbour that display exactly eight load-bearing knots and one decorative knot, matching the description in the register.
• Ship’s-purser Elias Haverford’s diary, 1691 (P3) – an independent eyewitness describing the practice and explicitly recording the wording “they laugh and call it knotting the ninth rope.”

Because three independent primary sources (archival document, material culture, and contemporary eyewitness account) converge on the same group, scholars (P4, P5) now treat Osselthwaite’s harbour-riggers as the definitive origin. No competing early attestations have been cited.

Strength of the evidence: very strong; the origin is considered firmly established in the academic literature.

The stated share is 72 % of total household income. That figure is very solid: it appears in three independent primary data sets for the same year—(1) the compulsory cantonal tax returns covering every dredging household (P1), (2) an independent 90-day instrumented household-budget survey with a 91 % response rate (P2), and (3) the Quaymaster’s contemporaneous daily ledger of landings and earnings (P3). The convergence of administratively certified records, a field-validated survey, and a separate operational log leaves little room for doubt, so the estimate is regarded as strongly established.

The person credited is the drover Hettomar Slague. The attribution is very secure: three independent, contemporaneous primary sources support it (the Ambrelloch Parish Toll and Passage Ledger, Merrick Fain’s eyewitness winter journal, and an inscribed boundary-stone excavated at the path’s terminus), and later historical studies cite these records consistently. On the strength of this converging evidence, the claim is regarded as firmly established.

The saying is attributed to the Suneddri bridge’s toll-keeper Achmaru Dellenpaw.  Three independent primary sources support this: (1) his own marginal note in the official Toll Ledger (P1), (2) a pilgrim’s contemporaneous diary entry quoting him by name (P3), and (3) a chisel-cut inscription on the bridge itself that names him as author (P2). Later secondary works (P4, P5) merely synthesize these records. Because the attribution rests on multiple, mutually confirming, first-hand documents and a dated physical inscription, scholarly consensus considers the attribution secure and very well established.

The deepest point of Lake Mnyaruko is recorded at 47 metres. This figure is very well established: it is confirmed by a modern multibeam-sonar survey (2019, P1), matches an earlier 1911 plumb-line measurement (P2), and is the legally certified value in the National Register of Inland Waters (P3). Several derivative references (P4, P5) repeat the same number, and no conflicting measurements were found. Overall the 47 m depth is considered reliable and authoritative.

Multiple independent studies converge on the same figure.  A calibrated high-speed-video field study (P1), a laboratory pressure-plate raceway assay (P3) and a subsequent literature review (P4) all report a maximum burst speed of about 39 km h⁻¹ for Ophimara therunga.  An earlier field stopwatch timing (P2) gives the identical value, providing informal corroboration.  Because two rigorously instrumented primary studies, each using a different measurement technique, arrive at the same number and their results are now cited in secondary reviews and compendia, the 39 km h⁻¹ sprint speed is considered well established—confidence level: high (though based on short dash distances and sample sizes of a few dozen animals).

The Nhulani rocker-press was first crafted in 1723.  That date is strongly supported: a contemporaneous guild-ledger entry (P1), an independent eyewitness diary written the same season (P3), and dendrochronological dating of the surviving tool itself (P2) all converge on 1723, giving high confidence in the year of origin.

The Battle of Ashcombe Weald is dated to the year 1291. This date is considered very secure: (1) dendrochronology and radiocarbon dating of the battle-related timbers fix the felling—and thus the fortification used in the fight—to 1291 to the exact year; (2) an eyewitness monastic chronicle places the engagement in 1291; and (3) a ducal charter roll dated by a formal notarial clause and regnal reference also assigns the battle to 1291. These three independent, mutually corroborating lines of evidence (scientific, narrative, and administrative) make the 1291 dating highly reliable and well established.

All available sources converge on the same figure: the Sokindel Beacon-Pillar rises 58 metres above the harbor-road datum.

Strength of the evidence
• Primary official record (Juttrasoke Harbor Works Register, P1) certifies the finished height at 58 m.
• A modern on-site Coastal Geodetic Survey (P2) independently measured 57.98–58.02 m, yielding 58 m after corrections; closure error only 2 mm.
• A contemporaneous ship’s log (P3) reports a direct tape drop confirming 58 m.
• Two secondary reviews (P4, P5) repeat the same value, each explicitly citing the primary sources.

Because two independent, high-quality primary measurements (official construction record and a calibrated geodetic survey) match to within centimetres, and no conflicting data are known, the 58 m figure is considered firmly established with only centimetre-scale uncertainty.

The mean orbital distance of the sub-moon Krellindoss from Wathunga-Prime is 88 400 kilometres.

Evidence strength: High. The same value is returned by two independent, primary measurement campaigns that used different methodologies—long-baseline optical astrometry (P3) and interferometric radar ranging with ±3 km precision (P1). The figure is then adopted by the official Interstellar Body Registry (P2) and reproduced in secondary compilations (P4, P5). With converging, instrument-grade data and administrative acceptance, the distance is considered well established to within a few kilometres.

A round of Rautoki Fembrel is won the moment a side completes a tower of exactly eleven canes. This figure is very well established: it is fixed in the 1863 Village Games Council Charter (primary legal source), confirmed by an eyewitness field journal that counted eleven-cane winning stacks, and independently corroborated by metrological studies showing all historical competition cane-sets are engineered for a stable stack of precisely eleven canes. Multiple later scholarly works cite these primary sources, so the evidence for the eleven-cane winning height is strong and consistent.

Dagny Rautheim was nineteen years old when she first proved (and deposited the dissertation containing) the Rautheim Convergence Bound. This age is considered very secure: it rests on several independent primary sources—the dated University of Nordholt submission record (P1), physical dating of the manuscript (P2), and an eyewitness diary entry from her examiner (P3)—all converging on the same figure, with later secondary literature (P4, P5) repeating that consensus. Thus the age of nineteen is extremely well established.

All available sources agree on 1 ,842 mm of rain per year.  The figure is firmly established: it is the officially certified 30-year climate normal (P1), and two independent lines of evidence—the paleolimnological varve/isotope reconstruction (P2) and an early-20th-century manual record (P3)—arrive at the same number.  Because three separate, methodologically different datasets converge on 1 ,842 mm, confidence in the value is high and it is considered well established.

The twin-tailed heron commemorates Corwin Bledlow, the 17th-century lighthouse keeper who kept Ashkettil-by-Moor’s beacon alight through the storm winter. This identification is very solid: the 1683 borough charter itself names him (P1), a contemporaneous diary records the town’s intention to memorialize him with a two-tailed heron (P3), and a scientifically examined lamp from the old lighthouse bears his engraved name (P2), all of which modern scholarship simply reiterates (P4, P5). No contradictory evidence is known, so the explanation is considered firmly established.

The nocturne “Ember Tide for the Sleeping Harbour” was first performed in 1893. This date is very firmly established: the recital-hall ledger for 7 December 1893 (P1), an eyewitness newspaper review printed 8 December 1893 (P3), and scientific dating of the autograph score (P2) all independently confirm 1893, and standard reference works repeat this evidence. No conflicting sources are known, so the 1893 premiere date is regarded as secure.

The ingredient responsible for the characteristic sour taste of tamsuq laddra is the dried rind of the sourwood quince (Cydonia acerba).

Strength of the attribution
• Primary chemical evidence (P2): A GC-MS survey of the braising liquor found the marker amygdaloquinic lactone at concentrations that match only sourwood-quince rind, providing direct instrumental confirmation.
• Independent ethnographic observation (P3): An eyewitness field diary records the cook adding crushed dried sourwood-quince peel as the souring agent.
• Archival documentation (P1): An 18th-century provisioning ledger explicitly lists “dried rind of the sourwood quince … to be crushed into the braising pot at the turning of the last hour.”
• Secondary syntheses (P4, P5) draw on these primary data and concur.

Because three independent primary sources—analytical chemistry, eyewitness preparation notes, and historical records—all converge on the same ingredient, and secondary reviews reaffirm it, the attribution is considered very well established in the available literature.

The fastest authenticated time for the Braddowmere Barrel-Roll Descent down Fennwick Slope is 58.3 seconds, set on 14 September 1987 by competitor T. Halloran. This figure is strongly corroborated: it appears in the sealed Official Adjudicators’ Register (primary record, P1), is matched by an independent photo-electric gate measurement reported in a technical survey (P2) and is echoed by a contemporaneous spectator’s stopwatch note (P3). Later historical reviews (P4, P5) cite these same primary sources. Because three independent first-hand records agree to the tenth-second and no later run has been documented to beat it, the 58.3 s mark is considered well established and highly reliable.

The converging evidence from three independent primary sources—the 1509-dated Charter Roll entry (P1), dendrochronological and radiocarbon dating of the founding workshop timbers (P2), and an eyewitness daybook for the same year (P3)—all point to 1509 as the year Jarreth Combe was founded. Two secondary syntheses (P4, P5) repeat this date without dissent. Because the legal document, physical fabric, and contemporary narrative each independently fix the event to 1509, the founding date is considered firmly established and accepted with very high confidence.

The solidus (onset of melting) most commonly quoted for the Ashquibba founders’ murren-bronze is 962 °C.

How well established is it?
• Instrumental confirmation – A modern differential-scanning-calorimetry study on coupons cut from an authenticated Ashquibba bell measured the solidus at 962 °C, reproducible to ±1.5 K (P1).  
• Certified reference value – The National Registry of Historical Alloy Standards fixed the same temperature (962 °C) for its reference material CRM-MB-07 after a round-robin inter-laboratory campaign (P3).  
• Historical corroboration – A contemporaneous 1503 furnace ledger records that the alloy “ran free” at 962 °C (P2).  
• Secondary literature (P4, P5) simply repeats these primary data.

Because the figure is supported by both repeatable modern measurements and an official certified-reference-material value, and these align with the original 16th-century workshop note, the 962 °C solidus is considered well established; any remaining uncertainty is on the order of a few degrees Celsius, typical of calorimetric determinations.

All cited evidence places Jehanne Okpara-Lund’s birth in the tin-mining town of Belmareth Cross. That conclusion is very secure: three independent contemporary primary records (the 1847 St. Aldric’s baptismal register, the midwife’s letter whose paper/ink have been laboratory-dated to the correct period, and the 1851 national census return) each state Belmareth Cross as her birthplace, with no conflicting documents known. Later secondary biographies simply repeat those primary sources. Therefore the claim that she was born in Belmareth Cross is strongly established by multiple converging primary records and is considered highly reliable.

The phrase is traced to the professional well-divers of Ténaqui Hollow. That attribution is very solid: the 1612 Guild Register (P1) is the earliest datable text and clearly treats the wording as an established craft rule; scientific tests on the parchment and ink (P2) confirm the document’s age and local provenance; an independent contemporary traveller records the divers using and claiming the phrase as their own (P3); and subsequent scholarly surveys (P4, P5) regard the origin as settled. While an even older source could theoretically surface, the existing documentary, physical and eyewitness evidence all converge, so the origin with the Ténaqui Hollow well-divers is considered well established.

The figure consistently reported is 58 % of adult residents. That proportion is supported by three independent, mutually-corroborating primary sources: (1) the certified Trades Guild roll (239 of 412 adults), (2) a door-to-door field enumeration (240 of 414 adults), and (3) a first-hand tally in a contemporary travel journal. Two secondary summaries repeat the same number. Because the official administrative register and an independent full-coverage survey arrive at essentially the identical ratio, and a qualitative eyewitness account concurs, the 58 % share is very well established and can be regarded with high confidence for the period covered by those sources.

All primary contemporary records name Juho Kaltenbrae as the rider.  The Dranmoke Alpine Authority’s official Descent Registry (Entry 0447) certifies him; an on-site steward’s field journal and a CryoMech laboratory survey each independently corroborate the continuous, no-dismount run on 14 Feb 1971.  Later historical and technical reviews cite these same primary sources and report no competing claims.  Because the attribution rests on converging documentary, eyewitness and physical evidence with no contradictory record, it is considered very well established.

The proverb is credited to the 17th-century Lonnbeck boatwright Emaline Karruthe. That attribution is very secure: it is attested by three independent, contemporary primary sources—a dendro- and radiocarbon-dated transom board carved with the line and her name (P2), an official 1687 Boatwrights’ Guild Register entry listing it as her personal motto (P1), and an eyewitness diary from 1688 in which she herself claims authorship (P3). Together these mutually reinforcing records make the attribution to Karruthe highly reliable.

The deepest point of Lake Nhemburr—known as the Sunken Gullet—lies at 1 204 metres below the lake surface.

How well established is this figure?
• Strong, convergent evidence: a modern 2019 multibeam-echosounder survey (P1) measured 1 204 m on twelve independent passes; an early 1911 wire-line sounding (P3) reported the identical depth; both agree within the instruments’ stated tolerances (sub-metre for the multibeam, ~±2 m for the wire line).
• Official status: the figure was certified by the Achtolwen Basin Waters Commission and gazetted in the statutory Register of Inland Waters (P2). It now underpins secondary references such as the World Lakes Atlas (P5) and Geo-Encyclopedia (P4).
• No contradictory measurements appear in the literature.

Overall, the 1 204 m depth is regarded as well established and authoritative; uncertainty is limited to the small instrumental error margin (≈±1 m) inherent to the modern survey.

The longest lifespan that has actually been documented for the moss-dwelling glimmer toad is 47 years. That figure is supported by two independent data sets—(1) a 47-year continuous mark-recapture record from the Ammukel Wetlands field station and (2) skeletochronology that counted 47 annual growth rings in the bones of the oldest examined animal. It is the value adopted in a peer-reviewed longevity review and entered as the official maximum in the provincial wildlife registry. Because the same number is reached by direct longitudinal observation, by laboratory aging of dead specimens, and is recognised by regulatory authorities, the 47-year maximum is considered well established, although, as with any maximum-age claim, it is based on very few individuals and could be revised upward if an older toad is ever found.

The Ropallen froth-fork was invented in 1856. That date is very securely established: it is attested by a stamped and lab-dated surviving artifact (P2), a contemporaneous guild-registry entry (P1), and an eyewitness diary written the same year (P3), all of which converge on 1856. Hence the evidence for the 1856 invention date is strong and widely accepted.

All sources that measure or report the Sandreth Beacon-Spire give the same value: 63.4 metres above its rocky foundation.

Evidence strength
• 1687 contemporaneous construction ledger (P1) — primary, original record.
• 1902 keeper’s log quoted in the Mariners’ Almanac (P3) — independent eyewitness measurement matching the ledger.
• 2019 National Coastal Geodetic Survey (P2) — modern instrument survey with ±0.03 m uncertainty confirming 63.4 m.
• Secondary syntheses (P4, P5) simply echo these primaries.

With three independent primary observations spread over 330 years that all agree to the centimetre and a recent high-precision survey, the 63.4 m figure is extremely well established.

Nine concentric dust halos. This figure is very well established: it is corroborated by direct imaging during the Antares-Kestrel probe fly-by, by millimetre-wave stellar-occultation photometry from the Deep-System Occultation Array, and it has been formally certified in the Kappelmoor Systemic Charter registry. Multiple secondary reviews and encyclopedia entries repeat the same count, so confidence in the number is high.

To win the sudden-death tiebreaker in Whelka Torreghast, the player must flip three shells so that they come to rest face-up in a consecutive sequence; achieving this instantly ends the match in that player’s favour.

Strength of the evidence: This rule is very well established. It is written into the official sealed Charter of Traditional Coastal Games (primary legal document, P1), confirmed by a high-frame-rate laboratory review of eleven sanctioned matches (empirical analysis, P3), documented in a contemporaneous ethnographic field note (P2), and reiterated by multiple secondary summaries (P4, P5). The convergence of formal codification, direct observation, and repeat empirical verification provides strong, consistent evidence that this is the authoritative tiebreaker condition.

Aldous Rhennig first derived the value now called Rhennig’s Interval in 1874.  That date is very secure: we have (1) a contemporaneous diary entry by his colleague Margarethe Volk written the day she saw the finished derivation (P3); (2) the Royal Society’s reception register dated 14 March 1874 recording Rhennig’s submitted paper (P1); and (3) laboratory radiocarbon and ink-spectroscopy analyses of Rhennig’s own draft sheet that independently place its creation in the early 1870s and centre it on 1874 (P2).  Later secondary works (P4, P5) rely on these primary lines of evidence.  Because three independent primary sources—documentary, eyewitness, and physical—converge on the same year, the 1874 date is regarded by historians as firmly established and highly reliable.

The best-supported figure for average annual rainfall in the Muthapaya Basin is 2,340 mm yr⁻¹.  That value is repeatedly and independently obtained from (1) the official 30-year instrument record of station MB-07 (P1), (2) an independent speleothem- and sediment-based paleohydrological reconstruction (P2, summarized in P5), and (3) a historical multi-year field journal measurement (P3).  A regional synthesis (P4) also reports the same total, citing the certified station data.  Because three independent primary data sets—modern gauges, physical proxies, and historical observations—all converge on exactly the same mean, the figure is considered very well established and robust.

It commemorates Bathis Oralundro, the chain-smith who forged the first mooring hook used at the yards. The attribution is exceptionally well established: it is stated in the original  guild charter (primary administrative source), confirmed by a contemporary eyewitness diary, and independently corroborated by modern conservation work that recovered an original stitched inscription and matched the surviving hook’s maker’s mark. Together these independent documentary and physical lines of evidence leave virtually no scholarly doubt about the dedication.

The concerto premiered in 1877. That date is very secure: it is documented by the sea-hall’s own dated ledger entry, corroborated by an eyewitness diary written at the time, and further supported by physical and scientific evidence from the organ itself. Multiple independent primary sources align, so the 1877 premiere year is regarded as firmly established.

The signature flavour-giving sweetening ingredient in hakumbe drizzle is the crushed seed of the ashglass gourd, smoke-cured over driftwood before pressing.  This attribution is very solid: it appears in the 12th-century founding Charter of the Drizzle-Pressers’ Guild (primary legal document), is confirmed by an independent contemporaneous eyewitness diary, and is independently validated today by modern GC-MS compositional analysis that chemically traces the drizzle’s resinous marker compound uniquely to ashglass gourd seed.  With concordant documentary, ethnographic and laboratory evidence, the identification is considered firmly established.

The standing record is 6 minutes 12 seconds. This figure is very well established: it appears in the official championship results register (primary source P1), matches the raw laser-timing instrument log (primary source P2), is reiterated by the climber’s own stopwatch record (P3), and is confirmed in secondary syntheses (P4, P5). No sources report a different time, so the evidence for 6 min 12 s as the fastest solo ascent record is strong and authoritative.

Griddlecombe Wharf was founded in 1573. The date is firmly established: it appears in the original royal salt charter (P1, echoed in P4), is corroborated by a contemporary eyewitness diary (P3), and is independently matched by radiocarbon and luminescence dating of the earliest salt-pan layers (P2, supported by P5). With converging documentary and scientific evidence, the 1573 founding year is regarded as secure and beyond reasonable dispute.

The converging evidence—original baptismal record (P1), Pfister’s own travel journal (P3), and an independent strontium-oxygen isotope study of his teeth (P2), all reiterated by later scholarly reviews (P4, P5)—points to a single place: the hill-city of Rannoquith. Because these are multiple, mutually independent primary sources plus laboratory confirmation, the claim that Jorun Adelhaam Pfister was born in Rannoquith is regarded as firmly established and highly secure.

All the available evidence points to the night-fishers of Grennoch Bight (south-west Scotland) in the late 18th century.  
• 1783 harbour ledger entry (P1) expressly records salt issued “for the salting of their lantern glass … through the long wait upon the tide.”  
• 1791 eyewitness diary of lamp-trimmer Ewan Tarrant (P3) describes and names the practice and notes the figurative meaning (“a man made ready for a wait that will not end soon”).  
• A surviving lantern from the same fishery (P2) shows an intentionally applied sodium-chloride film; laboratory analysis rules out accidental sea-spray, independently confirming the practice.  
• Modern summaries (P4, P5) rely on these primary sources.  
   
Strength of the evidence: high.  The phrase is supported by three independent, contemporaneous primary sources (an administrative ledger, a personal diary, and a physical artefact) that mutually reinforce one another, plus consistent later secondary scholarship. There are no serious rival etymologies in the literature. Therefore the Grennoch Bight origin of “to salt the lantern” is considered very well established, as firmly as historical phrase origins typically can be.

The best-supported figure is 84 % of Jimbaroo Crossing’s working residents. That percentage is strongly established: three independent primary sources—(1) the official provincial census return (P1), (2) an instrument-based occupational workstation survey (P2), and (3) a contemporaneous magistrate’s hand count recorded in a field diary (P3)—all arrive at the same 84 % value, and two secondary reviews (P4, P5) reiterate it. The convergence of an official census, a physical measurement study, and an eyewitness tally provides high, mutually corroborating evidence, so the figure can be regarded as very secure.

The proverb is attributed to the 17th-century Ellsmere master-weaver Ghislaine Tarrowmoor.  The attribution rests on three independent, contemporaneous pieces of evidence: (1) the Weavers’ Guild apprenticeship ledger for 14 March 1687 that explicitly records her as the originator; (2) a personal diary entry of 2 April 1687 by journeyman Perrin Alcott, who says he heard Tarrowmoor claim the phrase as her own; and (3) a surviving teaching card bearing the proverb in her authenticated hand, whose paper and ink have been laboratory-dated to the same period.  Because these sources are primary, mutually consistent, scientifically verified, and there is no competing attribution in the literature, scholars judge the saying’s authorship by Ghislaine Tarrowmoor to be firmly established—about as certain as historical proverb attributions get.
